1	---
2	name: brainstorming
3	description: "You MUST use this before any creative work - creating features, building components, adding functionality, or modifying behavior. Explores user intent, requirements and design before implementation."
4	---
5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough

The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.

118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding

134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:

136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.

202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
340

steps.message:
Here's the design.

**Approach.** A filter bar sits inside the existing panel, between the intro and the table. It has two Selects with labels above them:

- **Event:** "All events" plus the nine types, as they appear in the data.
- **Date range:** "Last 7 days", "Last 30 days", or "Last 90 days" (the default).

Changing either one filters the table straight away by hiding rows that don't match. Nothing re-renders, nothing submits, and the page never navigates. Ranges are counted back from the viewer's current time and compared against the UTC `when` field.

Under the bar, a polite live region reads "Showing 4 of 311 events", with locale number grouping. Screen readers announce it without moving focus. When nothing matches, one full-width row says "Matching events will appear here." The bar is in the HTML with `hidden`, and the JS turns it on. With JS off the page looks exactly as it does today, and the existing gap goes on the follow-up list as agreed.

**Styling.** I'll add a `:root` block with token values taken from 01-foundations. The new CSS uses only those tokens: label to control `--space-4`, the input surface spec, `--type-label`, a `:focus-visible` ring from `--border-focus`, and wrapping so it still works at 320px.

**Files and commits:**

1. `refactor: use design tokens in activity page styles`. Adds the `:root` tokens to `public/activity.css` and switches the existing raw values to them. The page should look the same afterwards.
2. `feat: filter account activity by event type and date range`. Touches `public/activity.html` (bar markup and live region), `public/activity.css` (bar styles), and `public/activity.js` (filter logic, count, empty row).

I expect about 150 lines in total. No new dependencies, and no changes to file names or paths.

**Testing.** There's no test suite, so I'll check it by hand:

- Open the page from disk in Safari and Firefox.
- Try every event type and every range, a few combinations, and a combination that matches nothing, and check the count each time.
- Tab through the controls with the keyboard only.
- Confirm VoiceOver announces the count.
- Narrow the window to 320px.
- Load the page with JS disabled.

results.content:
# 01 Foundations

These are the design tokens every page under `public/` draws from. Pages
reference tokens through CSS custom properties declared in the shared token
sheet; a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a
review comment. When a value you need is missing, add a token here first, then
reference it.

Tokens come in two layers. Palette tokens name a raw value and never carry
meaning. Semantic tokens name a role (surface, border, text, accent, state) and
point at a palette token per theme. Page CSS uses semantic tokens; palette
tokens appear only in this file and in the token sheet.

## Color palette

Twelve hues, eleven steps each. Steps below 500 are tints for surfaces and
borders; 500 is the reference fill; steps above 500 are for text and pressed
states. Contrast pairs that pass WCAG AA are listed under Semantic colors; do
not invent new pairings in page CSS.

| `--text-secondary` | `slate-600` | `slate-300` | Helper text, metadata |
| `--text-tertiary` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Placeholders, timestamps |
| `--text-disabled` | `slate-400` | `slate-600` | Disabled labels and values |
| `--text-inverse` | `#ffffff` | `slate-900` | Text on inverse and filled surfaces |
| `--text-link` | `blue-600` | `blue-400` | Inline links |
| `--text-link-hover` | `blue-700` | `blue-300` | Inline link hover |
| `--accent-fill` | `blue-600` | `blue-500` | Primary buttons, checked controls |
| `--accent-fill-hover` | `blue-700` | `blue-400` | Primary button hover |
| `--accent-fill-pressed` | `blue-800` | `blue-300` | Primary button pressed |
| `--accent-subtle` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Accent backgrounds, info banners |
| `--danger-fill` | `red-600` | `red-500` | Destructive buttons |
| `--danger-fill-hover` | `red-700` | `red-400` | Destructive button hover |
| `--danger-text` | `red-700` | `red-300` | Error messages, invalid field text |
| `--danger-subtle` | `red-50` | `red-950` | Error banners, invalid field background |
| `--warning-text` | `amber-800` | `amber-300` | Warning messages |
| `--warning-subtle` | `amber-50` | `amber-950` | Warning banners |
| `--success-text` | `green-700` | `green-300` | Success messages |
| `--success-subtle` | `green-50` | `green-950` | Success banners |
| `--info-text` | `blue-700` | `blue-300` | Informational messages |
| `--info-subtle` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Informational banners |
| `--overlay-scrim` | `slate-900` at 48% | `slate-950` at 64% | Behind dialogs |

Approved contrast pairs (AA for body text): `--text-primary` on every surface
token; `--text-secondary` on `--surface-page`, `--surface-panel`,
`--surface-raised`; `--text-inverse` on `--accent-fill`, `--danger-fill`,
`--surface-inverse`. `--text-tertiary` passes AA only for large text and is
never used for content a user must read to complete a task.

## Spacing

One scale, used for padding, gaps, and margins alike. Steps are named by index,
not by size, so that the scale can be retuned without renaming.

| Token | rem | px | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|

Every transition is disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

## Breakpoints and grid

| Token | Min width | Columns | Gutter | Page margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--bp-xs` | 0 | 4 | 16px | 16px |
| `--bp-sm` | 480px | 4 | 16px | 20px |
| `--bp-md` | 768px | 8 | 24px | 32px |
| `--bp-lg` | 1024px | 12 | 24px | 40px |
| `--bp-xl` | 1280px | 12 | 32px | 48px |
| `--bp-2xl` | 1536px | 12 | 32px | auto, content capped at 1280px |

## Borders, icons, and opacity

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--border-width-hairline` | 1px | Dividers, panel outlines, input borders |
| `--border-width-thick` | 2px | Focus rings, selected cards, invalid inputs |
| `--border-width-heavy` | 4px | The active-tab indicator and left accents on banners |
| `--icon-xs` | 12px | Inline with caption text |
| `--icon-sm` | 16px | Inline with body text, inside small buttons |
| `--icon-md` | 20px | Default for buttons and inputs |
| `--icon-lg` | 24px | Navigation and empty-state accents |
| `--icon-xl` | 40px | Empty-state illustrations |
| `--opacity-disabled` | 0.48 | Only for imagery; disabled text uses `--text-disabled` |
| `--opacity-scrim` | 0.48 | Dialog scrim in the light theme |
| `--opacity-hover-overlay` | 0.04 | Hover overlay on images and avatars |
| `--opacity-pressed-overlay` | 0.08 | Pressed overlay on images and avatars |

## Data visualization

Charts use a separate categorical sequence so that series never borrow state
colors (a red series reads as an error). Use the sequence in order; past eight
series, group the remainder into "Other".

| Token | Light | Dark | Order |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--chart-1` | `blue-600` | `blue-400` | First series |
| `--chart-2` | `teal-600` | `teal-400` | Second series |
| `--chart-3` | `violet-600` | `violet-400` | Third series |
| `--chart-4` | `amber-600` | `amber-400` | Fourth series |
| `--chart-5` | `pink-600` | `pink-400` | Fifth series |
| `--chart-6` | `cyan-700` | `cyan-300` | Sixth series |
| `--chart-7` | `indigo-700` | `indigo-300` | Seventh series |
| `--chart-8` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Eighth series, and "Other" |

     - Two Selects with labels above them:
       - "Event": "All events" plus the nine types.
       - "Date range": "Last 7 days", "Last 30 days", "Last 90 days" (the default).
     - Changing either Select filters immediately by hiding rows. Nothing submits and the page never navigates.
     - Ranges count back from the viewer's current time and compare against the UTC `when` field.
     - A polite live region reads "Showing 4 of 311 events", with locale number grouping.
     - When nothing matches, one full-width row says "Matching events will appear here."
     - The bar is in the HTML with the `hidden` attribute, and the JS reveals it. With JS off the page stays as it is today.
     - The existing no-JS gap (the tbody is rendered by JS) is left alone and logged as a follow-up.

3	The shared components every page builds from. Each section lists the props the

9	`--border-focus` ring at a 2px offset on `:focus-visible`, never on mouse

1	# 03 Forms
2	
3	How fields, labels, help, validation, and saving behave on every form in the
4	app. These rules apply field by field and to the save behavior of a form as a
5	whole.
6	
7	## Labels and help
8	
9	- Every field has a visible label. Placeholder text is never a label and never
10	  holds information the user needs after they start typing.
11	- Labels sit above their control, left-aligned, in `--type-label`. The gap from
12	  label to control is `--space-4`.
13	- Checkbox and switch labels sit to the right of the control, and the whole
14	  label is clickable.
15	- Hint text sits between the label and the control in `--type-body-sm` and
16	  `--text-secondary`, and the control references it with
17	  `aria-describedby`.
18	- Mark required fields with "(required)" after the label when most fields are
19	  optional, or mark optional fields with "(optional)" when most are required.
20	  Never rely on an asterisk alone.
21	- Keep labels to a noun phrase: "Display name", not "Enter your display name".
22	
23	## Field sizing
24	
25	Size the control to the value it will hold, not to the container. A five-digit
26	number in a full-width input reads as a bug.
27	
28	| Field type | Control | Width token | Validation | Keyboard and input mode | Notes |
29	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
30	| Person name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 80 characters | autocomplete=name | Do not split into first and last unless a downstream system requires it |
31	| Display name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 50 characters, trimmed | autocomplete=nickname | Shown to other users |
32	| Email address | TextInput type=email | `lg` | Syntax check on blur, existence check on save | inputmode=email, autocomplete=email | Changing it sends a confirmation email |
33	| Phone number | TextInput type=tel | `sm` | E.164 after normalization | inputmode=tel, autocomplete=tel | Show the normalized form after blur |
34	| URL | TextInput type=url | `lg` | Absolute http or https | inputmode=url | Prefix https:// when the user omits a scheme |
35	| Password | TextInput type=password | `md` | Policy from the auth service | autocomplete=new-password | Show and hide toggle as an IconButton |
36	| One-time code | TextInput | `xs` | 6 digits | inputmode=numeric, autocomplete=one-time-code | Paste fills every box |
37	| Search | TextInput type=search | `lg` | none | enterkeyhint=search | Clear button inside the field |
38	| Integer quantity | TextInput type=number | `xs` | Min and max from the API | inputmode=numeric | No spinner arrows |
39	| Duration in minutes | TextInput type=number | `xs` | 1 to 1440 | inputmode=numeric | Suffix "min" inside the field |
40	| Currency amount | TextInput | `sm` | Two decimals, locale aware | inputmode=decimal | Currency symbol as a prefix |
41	| Percentage | TextInput | `xs` | 0 to 100 | inputmode=decimal | Suffix "%" |
42	| Date | Date picker | `sm` | Valid calendar date | Typed entry allowed | Format from 04 Content |
43	| Date range | Two date pickers | `sm each` | Start before end | Typed entry allowed | Presets in a Select beside it |
44	| Time | TextInput | `xs` | 24-hour or 12-hour per locale | inputmode=numeric | Never a Select of every minute |
45	| Time zone | Select searchable | `lg` | IANA zone id | Type-ahead | Default to the browser zone; show the UTC offset in each option |
46	| Language | Select | `md` | Supported locale list | Type-ahead | Each option in its own language |
47	| Country | Select searchable | `md` | ISO 3166 list | Type-ahead | Put the detected country first |
48	| Theme or appearance | RadioGroup | `n/a` | One of the listed values | Arrow keys | Options: Light, Dark, Match system |
49	| Single on or off setting saved with the form | Checkbox | `n/a` | none | Space toggles | Use Switch only when the change applies immediately |
50	| Single on or off setting applied immediately | Switch | `n/a` | none | Space toggles | Never inside a form that has a Save button |
51	| Several independent options | Checkbox list | `n/a` | Optional minimum | Space toggles | Fieldset with a legend |
52	| One of two to five options | RadioGroup | `n/a` | Required unless a default is safe | Arrow keys | Show every option |
53	| One of six or more options | Select | `md` | Required unless a default is safe | Type-ahead | Group long lists |
54	| Long free text | Textarea | `full` | Max length from the API | none | Counter when a max exists |
55	| Secret value, shown once | Read-only field with copy button | `lg` | none | Copy with one click | Mask after the first view |
56	| Secret value, regenerable | Read-only field plus Button | `lg` | Confirm before regenerating | none | Regenerating revokes the old value |
57	| Avatar or image | File input with preview | `n/a` | Type and size from the API | none | Show the current image beside the control |
58	| Color | Swatch picker | `n/a` | One of the palette tokens | Arrow keys | Never free-form hex |
59	| Tags | Combobox with chips | `lg` | Max count from the API | Enter adds, Backspace removes | Suggest existing tags first |
60	
61	## Validation
62	
63	- Validate on blur for format, on save for anything that needs the server.
64	  Never validate on every keystroke; the exception is a counter that shows the
65	  remaining characters.
66	- An invalid field shows the invalid state from 02 Components and a message
67	  directly below the control, in `--danger-text`, starting with the field
68	  name.
69	- On a failed save, move focus to the first invalid field and show a Banner
70	  with tone `danger` at the top of the form listing every invalid field as a
71	  link to that field.
72	- Keep what the user typed. Never clear a field because it failed validation.
73

111	## Saving
112	
113	- A form with a Save button saves every field at once. Show the button in its
114	  `loading` state while saving and keep it in place; do not move or resize it.
115	- Disable nothing while saving. If the user edits a field mid-save, the next
116	  save sends the new value.
117	- On success, show a Toast ("Settings saved") and keep the user where they
118	  were. Do not navigate away and do not scroll.
119	- When the form has unsaved changes and the user tries to leave, confirm with
120	  a Dialog: title "Discard unsaved changes?", actions "Keep editing" (primary)
121	  and "Discard" (quiet).
122	- Settings that take effect immediately use a Switch and never sit inside a
123	  form with a Save button. Mixing the two on one page is allowed only when the
124	  immediate settings are clearly separated from the saved ones.
125	- Secrets (API tokens, recovery codes) are never sent back to the server on
126	  save. They are read-only, shown masked after the first view, and changed only
127	  through their own regenerate action with a confirming Dialog.

135	| Enter | Submits the form | No effect | Opens or selects | Submits from any text field |

137	| Escape | Clears a search field | No effect | Closes the list | Closes an open Dialog |
138	| Arrow keys | Moves the caret | No effect | Moves through options | Moves within a RadioGroup |
139	| Home / End | Line start or end | No effect | First or last option | No effect |

1	# 04 Content and accessibility
2	
3	How the interface talks, and the accessibility bar every page clears before it
4	ships.
5	
6	## Voice
7	
8	Plain, direct, and calm. Write the way a helpful colleague would say it out
9	loud. Lead with what the user can do, not with what went wrong. Prefer short
10	sentences and common words; cut any word that does not change the meaning.
11	
12	- Address the user as "you". Refer to the product as "we" only in messages
13	  where we did something ("We sent a code to your email").
14	- Never blame the user. "That code has expired" rather than "You entered an
15	  expired code".
16	- No exclamation marks outside of genuinely celebratory moments, and there are
17	  very few of those in a settings page.
18	- No jargon the user did not introduce. "Sign in", not "authenticate".
19	
20	## Capitalization and punctuation
21	
22	- Sentence case everywhere: page titles, headings, labels, buttons, menu items,
23	  tab names, and table headers. Proper nouns keep their capitals.
24	- Buttons are verbs or verb phrases: "Save", "Regenerate token", "Discard".
25	  Never "OK" or "Yes" in a Dialog; repeat the action.
26	- No period at the end of a label, button, heading, or single-sentence hint.
27	  Use periods in messages and multi-sentence help.
28	- Use the serial comma. Use an en dash for ranges ("9–5") and an em dash with
29	  no spaces for breaks in a sentence, sparingly.
30	
31	## Terminology
32	
33	Use the preferred term; reviewers flag the avoided forms.
34	
35	| Preferred | Avoid | Notes |
36	|---|---|---|
37	| sign in | log in, login (as a verb), authenticate | "Sign-in" as a noun or adjective |
38	| sign out | log out, logout | "Sign-out" as a noun |
39	| sign up | register, create login | Only on the public site |
40	| account | profile (for account-level settings) | Profile means the public-facing identity |
41	| profile | account (for public-facing identity) | Display name and avatar live here |
42	| settings | preferences, options, configuration | One word for every settings surface |
43	| display name | username, handle, nickname | There are no usernames in this product |
44	| email address | e-mail, mail, email ID | "Email" alone is fine in a label |
45	| time zone | timezone, TZ | Two words |
46	| language | locale | Locale is an implementation term |
47	| theme | appearance mode, skin | Light, Dark, Match system |
48	| notifications | alerts, messages | Alerts are a different, admin-only feature |
49	| email notifications | email alerts | Matches the field label |
50	| push notifications | mobile alerts, device notifications | Only for the mobile app and browser push |
51	| weekly digest | weekly summary, newsletter | Not a marketing email |
52	| two-factor authentication | 2FA, MFA, two-step verification | "Two-factor auth" in tight labels |
53	| recovery codes | backup codes | Shown once at setup |
54	| session timeout | idle timeout, auto logout | Minutes of inactivity before sign-out |
55	| API token | API key, access token, secret | Shown once, then masked |
56	| regenerate | reset, rotate, refresh | For tokens and codes |
57	| delete | remove, erase | Delete is permanent; remove is for detaching |
58	| remove | delete (when nothing is destroyed) | Removing a member keeps their account |
59	| save | apply, submit, update | For forms with a Save button |
60	| cancel | abort, back | Leaves without saving |
61	| discard | throw away, lose | Only for unsaved changes |
62	| dialog | modal, popup | In documentation; never shown to users |
63	| banner | alert bar, notice | In documentation |
64	| toast | snackbar, notification | In documentation |
65	| required | mandatory, compulsory | "(required)" after a label |
66	| optional | not required | "(optional)" after a label |
67	| invalid | wrong, bad, incorrect | In documentation; messages describe the fix |
68	| expired | timed out | For codes and sessions |
69	| offline | disconnected, no connection | In messages |
70	| workspace | organization, team, tenant | The billing and membership unit |
71	| member | user (inside a workspace) | User is fine in documentation |
72	| owner | admin (for the billing owner) | Admins are a separate role |
73	| admin | administrator, superuser | Short form everywhere |

75	## Formats
76	
77	| Value | Format | Example (en-US) | Notes |
78	|---|---|---|---|
79	| Date | Locale medium date | Sep 14, 2026 | Never numeric-only in the interface |
80	| Date and time | Locale medium date, short time | Sep 14, 2026, 3:05 PM | Show the time zone when it differs from the user's |
81	| Relative time | Rounded, past only | 5 minutes ago | Switch to an absolute date after 7 days |
82	| Duration | Largest two units | 1 hr 20 min | Never "80 minutes" |
83	| Number | Locale grouping | 12,480 | Tabular figures in tables |
84	| Percentage | Up to one decimal | 12.5% | No space before % in en-US |
85	| Currency | Locale currency format | $1,250.00 | Always two decimals |
86	| File size | Binary units, one decimal | 2.4 MB | Use MB, not MiB, in the interface |
87	| Time zone | Zone name with UTC offset | Pacific Time (UTC−07:00) | Use the minus sign, not a hyphen |
88	| Phone | National format when local, else E.164 | (555) 010-4477 | Store E.164 |

90	## Accessibility checklist
91	
92	Every page clears every row before it ships. "How to check" is what reviewers
93	actually do.
94	
95	| Criterion | Level | Requirement | How to check |
96	|---|---|---|---|
97	| 1.1.1 Non-text content | A | Every meaningful image and icon has a text alternative; decorative ones are hidden | Inspect alt and aria-hidden on every img and svg |
98	| 1.3.1 Info and relationships | A | Headings, lists, tables, labels, and fieldsets are real elements, not styled divs | Read the page with styles disabled |
99	| 1.3.2 Meaningful sequence | A | DOM order matches visual order | Tab through the page and watch the focus order |
100	| 1.3.3 Sensory characteristics | A | Instructions do not rely on shape, position, or color alone | Read every instruction out of context |
101	| 1.3.4 Orientation | AA | Works in portrait and landscape | Rotate a tablet emulator |
102	| 1.3.5 Identify input purpose | AA | Personal-data fields carry autocomplete tokens | Check against the field table in 03 Forms |
103	| 1.4.1 Use of color | A | Color is never the only way to convey state | View in grayscale |
104	| 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | AA | 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text | Use only the approved pairs in 01 Foundations |
105	| 1.4.4 Resize text | AA | Usable at 200% browser zoom without loss | Zoom to 200% and complete the main task |
106	| 1.4.5 Images of text | AA | No text rendered as images | Search the page for text in img |
107	| 1.4.10 Reflow | AA | No horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px wide | Set the viewport to 320px |
108	| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | AA | 3:1 for control borders and focus indicators | Check input borders and the focus ring |
109	| 1.4.12 Text spacing | AA | No clipping with increased letter, word, and line spacing | Apply the text-spacing bookmarklet |
110	| 1.4.13 Content on hover or focus | AA | Tooltips are dismissible, hoverable, and persistent | Hover, then move into the tooltip, then press Escape |
111	| 2.1.1 Keyboard | A | Every action is reachable and operable by keyboard | Unplug the mouse |
112	| 2.1.2 No keyboard trap | A | Focus can always leave a component | Tab into and out of every widget |
113	| 2.4.1 Bypass blocks | A | A skip link reaches the main content | Press Tab once on load |
114	| 2.4.2 Page titled | A | The document title names the page and the product | Check the browser tab |
115	| 2.4.3 Focus order | A | Focus moves in a logical order | Tab through and note every jump |
116	| 2.4.4 Link purpose | A | Link text makes sense out of context | List every link and read it alone |
117	| 2.4.6 Headings and labels | AA | Headings and labels describe their content | Read the heading outline alone |
118	| 2.4.7 Focus visible | AA | The focus ring is always visible | Tab through on every surface color |
119	| 2.4.11 Focus not obscured | AA | Sticky headers and footers never hide the focused element | Tab to fields near the sticky footer |
120	| 2.5.3 Label in name | A | The accessible name contains the visible label | Compare labels with the accessibility tree |
121	| 2.5.7 Dragging movements | AA | Anything draggable has a non-drag alternative | Try every drag interaction by keyboard |
122	| 2.5.8 Target size | AA | Targets are at least 24 by 24 CSS px | Measure IconButtons and checkboxes |
123	| 3.1.1 Language of page | A | The html element has a lang attribute | Inspect the root element |
124	| 3.2.1 On focus | A | Focus never triggers a change of context | Tab through every field |
125	| 3.2.2 On input | A | Changing a field never navigates or submits on its own | Change every select and radio |
126	| 3.3.1 Error identification | A | Errors are identified in text | Submit the form empty |
127	| 3.3.2 Labels or instructions | A | Every field has a label and needed instructions | Read the field table in 03 Forms |
128	| 3.3.3 Error suggestion | AA | Error messages say how to fix the problem | Compare against the message catalog |
129	| 3.3.4 Error prevention | AA | Destructive and financial actions are confirmable | Trigger every delete and regenerate |
130	| 3.3.7 Redundant entry | A | Previously entered information is not requested again | Walk the longest flow twice |
131	| 3.3.8 Accessible authentication | AA | No cognitive test to sign in; paste is allowed | Paste into every password and code field |
132	| 4.1.2 Name, role, value | A | Custom widgets expose correct roles and states | Inspect switches, tabs, and accordions |
133	| 4.1.3 Status messages | AA | Toasts and inline status are announced without moving focus | Listen with a screen reader on save |

35	1. Events are retained for 90 days, then deleted server-side. The page never needs to page past 90 days.
36	2. One request returns every event in the window, newest first. The cap is 500 events per user; the largest real account has 311. The page may assume the whole window is already loaded.

5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist

90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.

93	**Spike:**

97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)

105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document

109	**Architectural:**

111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. 134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:

196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you

199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.

# 01 Foundations

These are the design tokens every page under `public/` draws from. Pages
reference tokens through CSS custom properties declared in the shared token
sheet; a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a
review comment. When a value you need is missing, add a token here first, then
reference it.

Tokens come in two layers. Palette tokens name a raw value and never carry
meaning. Semantic tokens name a role (surface, border, text, accent, state) and
point at a palette token per theme. Page CSS uses semantic tokens; palette
tokens appear only in this file and in the token sheet.

## Color palette

## Semantic colors

Each semantic token resolves to a palette token per theme. The dark theme is
not shipped yet, but its column is maintained so that pages written today do
not need a second pass.

| Token | Light | Dark | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--surface-page` | `slate-50` | `slate-950` | The page background behind every panel |
| `--surface-panel` | `#ffffff` | `slate-900` | Primary content panels |
| `--surface-raised` | `#ffffff` | `slate-800` | Menus, popovers, dialogs |
| `--surface-sunken` | `slate-100` | `slate-950` | Wells, code blocks, read-only fields |
| `--surface-hover` | `slate-100` | `slate-800` | Row and item hover |
| `--surface-selected` | `blue-50` | `blue-900` | Selected rows, active navigation items |
| `--surface-inverse` | `slate-900` | `slate-50` | Tooltips, toasts |
| `--border-subtle` | `slate-200` | `slate-800` | Dividers between related items |
| `--border-default` | `slate-300` | `slate-700` | Input borders, panel outlines |
| `--border-strong` | `slate-400` | `slate-600` | Borders that must read at a glance |
| `--border-focus` | `blue-500` | `blue-400` | Focus ring, 2px, offset 2px |
| `--text-primary` | `slate-900` | `slate-50` | Body text, headings |
| `--text-secondary` | `slate-600` | `slate-300` | Helper text, metadata |
| `--text-tertiary` | `slate-500` | `slate-400` | Placeholders, timestamps |
| `--text-disabled` | `slate-400` | `slate-600` | Disabled labels and values |
| `--text-inverse` | `#ffffff` | `slate-900` | Text on inverse and filled surfaces |
| `--text-link` | `blue-600` | `blue-400` | Inline links |
| `--text-link-hover` | `blue-700` | `blue-300` | Inline link hover |
| `--accent-fill` | `blue-600` | `blue-500` | Primary buttons, checked controls |
| `--accent-fill-hover` | `blue-700` | `blue-400` | Primary button hover |
| `--accent-fill-pressed` | `blue-800` | `blue-300` | Primary button pressed |
| `--accent-subtle` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Accent backgrounds, info banners |
| `--danger-fill` | `red-600` | `red-500` | Destructive buttons |
| `--danger-fill-hover` | `red-700` | `red-400` | Destructive button hover |
| `--danger-text` | `red-700` | `red-300` | Error messages, invalid field text |
| `--danger-subtle` | `red-50` | `red-950` | Error banners, invalid field background |
| `--warning-text` | `amber-800` | `amber-300` | Warning messages |
| `--warning-subtle` | `amber-50` | `amber-950` | Warning banners |
| `--success-text` | `green-700` | `green-300` | Success messages |
| `--success-subtle` | `green-50` | `green-950` | Success banners |
| `--info-text` | `blue-700` | `blue-300` | Informational messages |
| `--info-subtle` | `blue-50` | `blue-950` | Informational banners |
| `--overlay-scrim` | `slate-900` at 48% | `slate-950` at 64% | Behind dialogs |

Approved contrast pairs (AA for body text): `--text-primary` on every surface
token; `--text-secondary` on `--surface-page`, `--surface-panel`,
`--surface-raised`; `--text-inverse` on `--accent-fill`, `--danger-fill`,
`--surface-inverse`. `--text-tertiary` passes AA only for large text and is
never used for content a user must read to complete a task.

## Spacing

One scale, used for padding, gaps, and margins alike. Steps are named by index,
not by size, so that the scale can be retuned without renaming.

| Token | rem | px | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `--space-0` | 0 | 0 | Resetting inherited spacing |
| `--space-1` | 0.125 | 2 | Hairline offsets, icon nudges |
| `--space-2` | 0.25 | 4 | Gap between an icon and its label |
| `--space-3` | 0.375 | 6 | Padding inside badges and chips |
| `--space-4` | 0.5 | 8 | Gap between a label and its control |
| `--space-5` | 0.75 | 12 | Vertical gap between stacked fields |
| `--space-6` | 1 | 16 | Padding inside inputs and small cards |
| `--space-7` | 1.25 | 20 | Gap between buttons in a button row |
| `--space-8` | 1.5 | 24 | Padding inside panels |
| `--space-9` | 2 | 32 | Gap between panels |
| `--space-10` | 2.5 | 40 | Page gutter on tablet |
| `--space-11` | 3 | 48 | Page gutter on desktop |
| `--space-12` | 4 | 64 | Top margin above a page title |
| `--space-13` | 5 | 80 | Empty-state padding |
| `--space-14` | 6 | 96 | Marketing sections only |
| `--space-15` | 8 | 128 | Marketing sections only |

## Typography

One family for interface text and one for code. Sizes are set in rem so they
follow the user's browser setting.

| Role | Token | Size (rem) | Line height | Weight | Tracking |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Display | `--type-display` | 2.25 | 1.15 | 700 | -0.02em |
| Page title | `--type-title` | 1.5 | 1.25 | 650 | -0.01em |
| Heading 2 | `--type-h2` | 1.25 | 1.3 | 600 | -0.005em |
| Heading 3 | `--type-h3` | 1.0625 | 1.35 | 600 | 0 |
| Heading 4 | `--type-h4` | 0.9375 | 1.4 | 600 | 0.01em |
| Body large | `--type-body-lg` | 1.0625 | 1.6 | 400 | 0 |
| Body | `--type-body` | 0.9375 | 1.55 | 400 | 0 |
| Body small | `--type-body-sm` | 0.8125 | 1.5 | 400 | 0.005em |
| Label | `--type-label` | 0.875 | 1.4 | 500 | 0 |
| Caption | `--type-caption` | 0.75 | 1.4 | 400 | 0.01em |

Families: `--font-sans` is `"Inter", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI",

Menlo, monospace`. Numbers in tables use `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`.

# 03 Forms

How fields, labels, help, validation, and saving behave on every form in the
app. These rules apply field by field and to the save behavior of a form as a
whole.

## Labels and help

- Every field has a visible label. Placeholder text is never a label and never
  holds information the user needs after they start typing.
- Labels sit above their control, left-aligned, in `--type-label`. The gap from
  label to control is `--space-4`.
- Checkbox and switch labels sit to the right of the control, and the whole
  label is clickable.
- Hint text sits between the label and the control in `--type-body-sm` and
  `--text-secondary`, and the control references it with
  `aria-describedby`.
- Mark required fields with "(required)" after the label when most fields are
  optional, or mark optional fields with "(optional)" when most are required.
  Never rely on an asterisk alone.
- Keep labels to a noun phrase: "Display name", not "Enter your display name".

## Field sizing

Size the control to the value it will hold, not to the container. A five-digit
number in a full-width input reads as a bug.

| Field type | Control | Width token | Validation | Keyboard and input mode | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Person name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 80 characters | autocomplete=name | Do not split into first and last unless a downstream system requires it |
| Display name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 50 characters, trimmed | autocomplete=nickname | Shown to other users |
| Email address | TextInput type=email | `lg` | Syntax check on blur, existence check on save | inputmode=email, autocomplete=email | Changing it sends a confirmation email |
| Phone number | TextInput type=tel | `sm` | E.164 after normalization | inputmode=tel, autocomplete=tel | Show the normalized form after blur |
| URL | TextInput type=url | `lg` | Absolute http or https | inputmode=url | Prefix https:// when the user omits a scheme |

1	# 03 Forms
2	
3	How fields, labels, help, validation, and saving behave on every form in the
4	app. These rules apply field by field and to the save behavior of a form as a
5	whole.
6	
7	## Labels and help
8	
9	- Every field has a visible label. Placeholder text is never a label and never
10	  holds information the user needs after they start typing.
11	- Labels sit above their control, left-aligned, in `--type-label`. The gap from
12	  label to control is `--space-4`.
13	- Checkbox and switch labels sit to the right of the control, and the whole
14	  label is clickable.
15	- Hint text sits between the label and the control in `--type-body-sm` and
16	  `--text-secondary`, and the control references it with
17	  `aria-describedby`.
18	- Mark required fields with "(required)" after the label when most fields are
19	  optional, or mark optional fields with "(optional)" when most are required.
20	  Never rely on an asterisk alone.
21	- Keep labels to a noun phrase: "Display name", not "Enter your display name".

23	## Field sizing
24	
25	Size the control to the value it will hold, not to the container. A five-digit
26	number in a full-width input reads as a bug.
27	
28	| Field type | Control | Width token | Validation | Keyboard and input mode | Notes |
29	|---|---|---|---|---|---|
30	| Person name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 80 characters | autocomplete=name | Do not split into first and last unless a downstream system requires it |
31	| Display name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 50 characters, trimmed | autocomplete=nickname | Shown to other users |
32	| Email address | TextInput type=email | `lg` | Syntax check on blur, existence check on save | inputmode=email, autocomplete=email | Changing it sends a confirmation email |
33	| Phone number | TextInput type=tel | `sm` | E.164 after normalization | inputmode=tel, autocomplete=tel | Show the normalized form after blur |
34	| URL | TextInput type=url | `lg` | Absolute http or https | inputmode=url | Prefix https:// when the user omits a scheme |
35	| Password | TextInput type=password | `md` | Policy from the auth service | autocomplete=new-password | Show and hide toggle as an IconButton |
36	| One-time code | TextInput | `xs` | 6 digits | inputmode=numeric, autocomplete=one-time-code | Paste fills every box |
37	| Search | TextInput type=search | `lg` | none | enterkeyhint=search | Clear button inside the field |
38	| Integer quantity | TextInput type=number | `xs` | Min and max from the API | inputmode=numeric | No spinner arrows |
39	| Duration in minutes | TextInput type=number | `xs` | 1 to 1440 | inputmode=numeric | Suffix "min" inside the field |
40	| Currency amount | TextInput | `sm` | Two decimals, locale aware | inputmode=decimal | Currency symbol as a prefix |
41	| Percentage | TextInput | `xs` | 0 to 100 | inputmode=decimal | Suffix "%" |
42	| Date | Date picker | `sm` | Valid calendar date | Typed entry allowed | Format from 04 Content |
43	| Date range | Two date pickers | `sm each` | Start before end | Typed entry allowed | Presets in a Select beside it |
44	| Time | TextInput | `xs` | 24-hour or 12-hour per locale | inputmode=numeric | Never a Select of every minute |
45	| Time zone | Select searchable | `lg` | IANA zone id | Type-ahead | Default to the browser zone; show the UTC offset in each option |
46	| Language | Select | `md` | Supported locale list | Type-ahead | Each option in its own language |
47	| Country | Select searchable | `md` | ISO 3166 list | Type-ahead | Put the detected country first |

51	| Several independent options | Checkbox list | `n/a` | Optional minimum | Space toggles | Fieldset with a legend |

61	## Validation
62	
63	- Validate on blur for format, on save for anything that needs the server.
64	  Never validate on every keystroke; the exception is a counter that shows the
65	  remaining characters.
66	- An invalid field shows the invalid state from 02 Components and a message
67	  directly below the control, in `--danger-text`, starting with the field
68	  name.
69	- On a failed save, move focus to the first invalid field and show a Banner
70	  with tone `danger` at the top of the form listing every invalid field as a
71	  link to that field.
72	- Keep what the user typed. Never clear a field because it failed validation.

111	## Saving
112	
113	- A form with a Save button saves every field at once. Show the button in its
114	  `loading` state while saving and keep it in place; do not move or resize it.
115	- Disable nothing while saving. If the user edits a field mid-save, the next
116	  save sends the new value.
117	- On success, show a Toast ("Settings saved") and keep the user where they
118	  were. Do not navigate away and do not scroll.
119	- When the form has unsaved changes and the user tries to leave, confirm with
120	  a Dialog: title "Discard unsaved changes?", actions "Keep editing" (primary)
121	  and "Discard" (quiet).
122	- Settings that take effect immediately use a Switch and never sit inside a
123	  form with a Save button. Mixing the two on one page is allowed only when the
124	  immediate settings are clearly separated from the saved ones.
125	- Secrets (API tokens, recovery codes) are never sent back to the server on
126	  save. They are read-only, shown masked after the first view, and changed only
127	  through their own regenerate action with a confirming Dialog.

131	| Key | In a text field | On a checkbox or switch | In a select | On the form |
132	|---|---|---|---|---|
133	| Tab | Next field | Next field | Next field | Moves through fields in reading order |
134	| Shift+Tab | Previous field | Previous field | Previous field | Reverse order |
135	| Enter | Submits the form | No effect | Opens or selects | Submits from any text field |
136	| Space | Types a space | Toggles | Opens | No effect |
137	| Escape | Clears a search field | No effect | Closes the list | Closes an open Dialog |
138	| Arrow keys | Moves the caret | No effect | Moves through options | Moves within a RadioGroup |
139	| Home / End | Line start or end | No effect | First or last option | No effect |

336	# 04 Content and accessibility
337	
338	How the interface talks, and the accessibility bar every page clears before it
339	ships.
340	
341	## Voice
342	
343	Plain, direct, and calm. Write the way a helpful colleague would say it out
344	loud. Lead with what the user can do, not with what went wrong. Prefer short
345	sentences and common words; cut any word that does not change the meaning.
346	
347	- Address the user as "you". Refer to the product as "we" only in messages
348	  where we did something ("We sent a code to your email").
349	- Never blame the user. "That code has expired" rather than "You entered an
350	  expired code".
351	- No exclamation marks outside of genuinely celebratory moments, and there are
352	  very few of those in a settings page.
353	- No jargon the user did not introduce. "Sign in", not "authenticate".
354	
355	## Capitalization and punctuation
356	
357	- Sentence case everywhere: page titles, headings, labels, buttons, menu items,
358	  tab names, and table headers. Proper nouns keep their capitals.
359	- Buttons are verbs or verb phrases: "Save", "Regenerate token", "Discard".
360	  Never "OK" or "Yes" in a Dialog; repeat the action.
361	- No period at the end of a label, button, heading, or single-sentence hint.
362	  Use periods in messages and multi-sentence help.
363	- Use the serial comma. Use an en dash for ranges ("9–5") and an em dash with
364	  no spaces for breaks in a sentence, sparingly.

666	## Screen reader support
667	
668	Test with VoiceOver on Safari and NVDA on Firefox before shipping. A page
669	passes when a screen reader user can complete its main task without sighted
670	help, hears every validation message when it appears, and hears the save
671	confirmation without losing their place.
